results.name: Required sections present
results.criterion: The lesson has an H2 section for each of: what is RAG, why it matters, how it works, a worked example, limits, recap, a self-check quiz, and key words.

results.name: Short sentences
results.criterion: Average sentence length <= 15 words AND no sentence longer than 25 words.
evidence: (26 words) Indexing documents: Indexing (organizing and preparing documents so they can be searched quickly) means you collect your documents and split them into small pieces called chunks.

(31 words) Storing data: You store these embeddings in a searchable place called a vector database (a database [an organized collection of data stored in a computer] designed to search through meaning-based numbers).

(37 words) In this analogy, the LLM is the student, the textbook is the folder of documents, looking up the page is retrieval, adding notes to the answer sheet is augmentation, and writing the final exam answer is generation.
results.fix: Split every sentence longer than 25 words into two or three short sentences. One idea per sentence.

results.name: Plain-English readability
results.criterion: Flesch Reading Ease >= 60 on the lesson prose.

results.name: Right length for one sitting
results.criterion: Between 850 and 1800 words (~10-15 minutes of reading for a slow reader).

results.name: Self-check with answers
results.criterion: The quiz section has at least 3 questions and gives the answers.

results.name: No false or misleading claims
results.criterion: Every technical claim agrees with the reference facts. No listed misconception is stated or implied as true. Simplifications are allowed only if they do not create a wrong belief (e.g. 'the model learns your documents' is a FAIL, because RAG does not change the model).
results.reasoning: I checked all the specified negative constraints regarding common RAG misconceptions and verified the technical claims against the reference facts. The lesson accurately presents RAG without stating or implying any of the forbidden misconceptions, and all definitions align with the provided reference sheet.

results.name: All must-cover points taught
results.criterion: Every must-cover point in the reference is actually taught (explained, not just named).
results.reasoning: Every single must-cover point (M1 through M9) from the reference sheet is explicitly taught and explained in simple terms throughout the lesson, complete with clear definitions and a concrete use case.

results.name: Every technical term explained
results.criterion: Every technical or English-uncommon term is explained in simple words at or before its first use in the body (a glossary at the end alone does not count). Acronyms are expanded on first use.
results.reasoning: I checked every listed technical and uncommon term in the lesson. Each term is clearly defined in simple words right at or before its first appearance in the body text.

results.name: Concrete analogy and walk-through
results.criterion: The lesson has (a) at least one everyday analogy a young Indian learner would recognise, correctly mapped to RAG, AND (b) one concrete worked example that follows a single question through every step: preparing documents, retrieving, adding to the prompt, generating.
results.reasoning: I checked the lesson for an everyday analogy suitable for a young Indian learner and found the open-book exam analogy, which is correctly mapped to all parts of RAG. I also checked the concrete worked example about the college helpdesk bot, and it explicitly covers document preparation, retrieval, prompt augmentation, and LLM generation step by step.

results.name: Fits a non-native English beginner
results.criterion: Uses common, everyday English words; no idioms, slang, sarcasm or culturally obscure references; assumes no coding, maths beyond class 12, or prior AI knowledge; tone is encouraging and direct.
results.reasoning: I checked the lesson for idioms, slang, uncommon words, assumed coding/math knowledge, grammatical issues, and tone. The vocabulary is kept simple, technical terms are explicitly defined in-line or via glossary, grammar is straightforward and clean, and the tone directly addresses the learner using 'you' while maintaining a helpful, encouraging posture.

results.name: Builds step by step
results.criterion: Ideas are introduced before they are used; sections go from what -> why -> how -> example -> limits -> recap; each section links to the previous one; nothing is repeated without purpose.
results.reasoning: I checked the requested section ordering, the introduction of terms before usage, the logical flow and transitions between sections, and the purposeful placement of analogies. All items are fully satisfied and adhere strictly to the constraints.

change_log.change: Added simple explanations for technical terms like AI model, trained, training data, hallucinate, retrieval, generation, indexing, index, embedding, database, vector database, and prompt right at their first use in the body.
Added an everyday open-book exam analogy mapped to RAG before the worked example.
